facts.fact_text: The applicant organisation is a non-governmental human rights organisation.
On 6 May 2008, the applicant organisation applied to the Mayor of Yerevan, notifying its intention to hold a mourning march on the first anniversary of L.G.'s death.
The mourning march notified by the applicant organisation was planned to take place on 12 May 2008.
On 8 May 2008, the Mayor of Yerevan decided to ban the planned mourning march.
On 12 May 2008, the police prevented the organisers from holding the planned mourning march.
The Mayor of Yerevan's decision to ban the planned mourning march was made with reference to Section 9 § 4 (3) of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act.
The Mayor of Yerevan's decision to ban the planned mourning march was made with reference to Section 13 § 1 (3) of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act.

According to Section 9 § 4 (3) of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the competent authority may ban the holding of a public event if, according to credible data, it is aimed at forcibly overthrowing the constitutional order.

According to Section 9 § 4 (3) of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the competent authority may ban the holding of a public event if, according to credible data, it may lead to mass disorder and crime.

According to Section 9 § 4 (3) of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the competent authority may ban the holding of a public event if, according to credible data, it may lead to undermining national security, public order and the health and morality of society.

According to Section 9 § 4 (3) of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, data may be considered credible if the Police or the National Security Service under the Government of Armenia have issued an official opinion on the data.

According to Section 9 § 6 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, in cases where mass public events have turned into mass disorder resulting in human casualties, the competent authority may temporarily ban the holding of mass public events in order to prevent new crimes.

The Mayor of Yerevan's ban decision cited an official opinion of the Police dated 8 May 2008, stating that the mass public event held on 1 March 2008 turned into mass disorder resulting in human casualties.
The Mayor of Yerevan's ban decision cited the Police opinion concluding that it would be impossible to prevent new crimes if the planned mass public event were held.

The National Security Service of Armenia's opinion of 7 May 2008 stated that the National Security Service had credible and verified data showing that the planned mass public event, if allowed, would result in undermining national security.

The National Security Service of Armenia's opinion of 7 May 2008 stated that the planned mass public event, if allowed, would result in undermining public order and the health and morality of society.
The National Security Service of Armenia's opinion of 7 May 2008 stated that the planned mass public event, if allowed, would result in disorder and new crimes.
The death of L.G. on 12 May 2007 provoked an outcry among Armenian human rights groups and civil society.
On 6 May 2008, the applicant organisation applied to the Mayor of Yerevan, notifying its intention to hold a mourning march on the first anniversary of L.G.'s death.
The mourning march notified by the applicant organisation was planned to take place on 12 May 2008.
The mourning march notified by the applicant organisation was planned to take place from 8 p.m. to 9.30 p.m.
The mourning march notified by the applicant organisation was planned to start at Republic Square in Yerevan.
The mourning march notified by the applicant organisation was planned to continue through Nalbandyan Street in the direction of the police station.
On 8 May 2008, the Mayor of Yerevan decided to ban the planned mourning march.

The Mayor of Yerevan's ban decision cited an official opinion of the Police dated 8 May 2008, stating that the mass public event held on 1 March 2008 turned into mass disorder resulting in human casualties.
The Mayor of Yerevan's ban decision cited the Police opinion stating that not all the circumstances of the crime and offenders from the 1 March 2008 event had been disclosed.

The Mayor of Yerevan's ban decision cited the Police opinion stating that not all weapons and ammunition used at the 1 March 2008 event, whose circulation may pose danger to the lives and health of citizens, had been found in the course of the investigation.
The Mayor of Yerevan's ban decision cited the Police opinion concluding that it would be impossible to prevent new crimes if the planned mass public event were held.
The Mayor of Yerevan's ban decision cited an official opinion of the National Security Service of Armenia dated 7 May 2008.

The National Security Service of Armenia's opinion of 7 May 2008 stated that the National Security Service had credible and verified data showing that the planned mass public event, if allowed, would result in undermining national security.

The National Security Service of Armenia's opinion of 7 May 2008 stated that the planned mass public event, if allowed, would result in undermining public order and the health and morality of society.
The National Security Service of Armenia's opinion of 7 May 2008 stated that the planned mass public event, if allowed, would result in encroachments on constitutional rights and freedoms.
The National Security Service of Armenia's opinion of 7 May 2008 stated that the planned mass public event, if allowed, would result in disorder and new crimes.
On 12 May 2008, the police prevented the organisers from holding the planned mourning march.

According to Section 9 § 6 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, in cases where mass public events have turned into mass disorder resulting in human casualties, the competent authority may temporarily ban the holding of mass public events in order to prevent new crimes.

According to Section 9 § 6 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the temporary ban on mass public events may be imposed only given that other means of prevention have been exhausted.

According to Section 9 § 6 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the temporary ban on mass public events shall last until the circumstances of the crime and the identity of the offenders have been disclosed.
